platforms.title: Sore Throat Antibiotics: When Do You Actually Need Them?
platforms.meta_description: Most sore throats clear in a week and antibiotics cut about 16 hours. Learn the NICE FeverPAIN score, when a pharmacist can help, and the signs that mean 999.
platforms.body_html:
It starts as a scratch and by the next morning every swallow feels like glass. You look in the mirror, see red, swollen tonsils, and the first thought is a GP appointment and a course of antibiotics. The NICE guideline on sore throat starts from a different place. It reminds clinicians that acute sore throat is self-limiting and often triggered by a virus, and that most people get better within about a week without antibiotics, whether the cause is bacteria or a virus. The real question is not whether antibiotics are good, but whether your particular sore throat is one of the minority where they make a difference.

Why Does a Sore Throat Usually Not Need Antibiotics?

According to the NHS, sore throats are usually caused by viruses, like a cold or flu, or by smoking, and only very occasionally by bacteria. Antibiotics act on bacteria, so against a cold virus they do nothing at all. Even when bacteria are involved, the benefit is smaller than most people expect. NICE notes that antibiotics shorten symptoms by about 16 hours on average, and that most people feel better after one week with or without them. Set against that are side effects, particularly diarrhoea and nausea, and the fact that previous antibiotic use can leave you carrying resistant bacteria next time.

The bacterium that matters most is streptococcus, the cause of strep throat. People with a strep sore throat are the ones more likely to benefit from treatment, so NICE asks clinicians to use a scoring tool, either FeverPAIN or Centor, to work out who that is likely to be. Rapid strep A tests are not recommended for routine use in NICE's guidance, which is why the score carries so much weight in UK practice.

Score Yourself the Way a Clinician Would

FeverPAIN gives one point for each of these:

  • Fever in the previous 24 hours
  • Purulence, meaning pus on the tonsils
  • Attend rapidly, within 3 days of symptoms starting
  • Severely Inflamed tonsils
  • No cough or coryza (a runny, inflamed nose)

The NICE guideline links each band to how often streptococcus is found. A score of 0 or 1 is associated with a 13 to 18% likelihood, 2 or 3 with 34 to 40%, and 4 or 5 with a 62 to 65% likelihood of isolating streptococcus. The older Centor score, also defined in the NICE guideline, uses four points (tonsillar exudate, tender swollen glands at the front of the neck, a history of fever over 38 degrees Celsius, and no cough); 0 to 2 points carries a 3 to 17% likelihood and 3 or 4 points a 32 to 56% likelihood.

Notice what the cough item tells you. A sore throat that arrives with a cough and a streaming nose scores lower, because that pattern fits a cold virus.

What Happens When You Match the Treatment to the Score

NICE turns those bands into three routes. With a FeverPAIN score of 0 or 1, or a Centor score of 0 to 2, no antibiotic prescription is offered; the advice is about managing symptoms. With FeverPAIN 2 or 3, the clinician considers either no antibiotic or a back-up prescription, one you only collect if symptoms have not started to improve within 3 to 5 days or get much worse. With FeverPAIN 4 or 5, or Centor 3 or 4, an immediate prescription or a back-up prescription is considered. People who are very unwell or at high risk of complications are offered antibiotics straight away.

In England, you may not need a GP for this step. The NHS says a pharmacist can give the same antibiotic treatment as a GP for a sore throat if you need it, for adults and children aged 5 and over; children under 5 should be seen by a GP.

Whatever the score, the self-care is the same. NICE suggests paracetamol for pain or fever, or ibuprofen if preferred and suitable, plus enough fluids. Medicated lozenges with a local anaesthetic, an anti-inflammatory or an antiseptic may help adults a little; NICE found no evidence either way for plain sweets or mouthwashes. The NHS adds a gargle of half a teaspoon of salt dissolved in a glass of warm water, spat out afterwards, though children should not try this. Cool or soft foods, rest and avoiding smoky places also help.

Signs That Change the Plan

The NHS lists clear points for getting help. Call 999 or go to A&E if you or your child:

  • have difficulty breathing or are unable to swallow
  • are drooling, which can be a sign of not being able to swallow
  • make a high-pitched sound when breathing in (stridor)
  • have severe symptoms that are getting worse quickly

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or use NHS 111 if you have a very high temperature or feel hot, cold and shivery, show signs of dehydration such as dark, strong-smelling pee, or have a weakened immune system, for example from diabetes or chemotherapy. See a GP if the sore throat has not improved after a week, if you get sore throats often, or if a lump or mouth ulcer lasts more than 3 weeks.

The One Number to Remember

If you keep only one thing from this, make it the score: a sore throat that comes with a cough and a runny nose sits at the low end, while fever, pus on the tonsils and no cough push it towards the 4 or 5 band where an antibiotic is most likely to earn its side effects.

This article is general information and does not replace advice from your pharmacist or GP.

Sources: NICE guideline NG84, "Sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing" (recommendations and terms used, published 26 January 2018); NHS, "Sore throat" (page last reviewed 8 April 2024).
